question_en: An agile leader notices that one team member consistently fails to complete the deliverables on time. The agile leader suspects that this team member does not have the proper training. What should the agile leader do?

options_en.A: Review the definition of done (DoD) with the team so that everyone understands what the team must deliver in this sprint.
options_en.B: Reassign the task to another team member and require the team member to complete training
options_en.C: Speak directly with the team member about improvements and commit to an agreed-upon time frame.
options_en.D: Use the retrospective meeting to remind the entire team that they must complete all deliverables in each sprint

explanation_en: The agile leader should speak directly with the underperforming team member, provide constructive feedback, and agree on a realistic improvement timeline. This demonstrates respect, empathy, and commitment to helping the team member grow. Direct conversation enables understanding of root causes and development of an achievable improvement plan.

question_en: A new offshore call center project is vital for a company's branch offices. The project is at the end of the planning phase when the project manager is informed by the sponsor that the project will be delayed due to reprioritization. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Create a messaging group chat with the branch office stakeholders to inform them about the project delay.
options_en.B: Schedule a video conference to inform the branch office stakeholders about the project delay.
options_en.C: Send an official project memo to inform the branch office stakeholders about the project delay.
options_en.D: Include the project delay in the monthly progress report for the branch office stakeholders.

explanation_en: When a vital project is delayed due to reprioritization at the end of planning, the project manager should schedule a video conference to inform branch office stakeholders. Video conferencing enables two-way communication, clarity, and immediate response to concerns. A messaging group chat (A) is too informal. Sending an official memo (C) is one-way communication. Including it in the monthly report (D) delays the message unnecessarily.

question_en: A company's project management office (PMO) is incorporating more adaptive technologies and has hired a new project manager with hybrid project management experience. The team is slow in adopting the new methodology and has not been updating project artifacts in a timely manner. Which action should the project manager take to improve the team's performance?

options_en.A: Set up a training session for all project team members
options_en.B: Speak individually with each project team member about making the needed updates
options_en.C: Send an email asking all project team members to complete updates at the end of the day
options_en.D: Reach out to the functional managers for support

explanation_en: When a PMO is incorporating adaptive technologies and the team is slow to adopt the new methodology, the project manager should set up a training session for all team members. Training addresses the root cause—lack of understanding—and builds capability for the new approach. Speaking individually with each member (B) is time-consuming and less effective. Sending an email about updates (C) is passive. Reaching out to functional managers (D) does not build team capability.

question_en: A project manager just finished a meeting to identify the main stakeholders of the project. What should the project manager do next?

options_en.A: Monitor all stakeholders.
options_en.B: Analyze the stakeholders.
options_en.C: Keep all stakeholders informed.
options_en.D: Engage the stakeholders.

explanation_en: After identifying the main stakeholders, the project manager should next analyze the stakeholders. Stakeholder analysis determines interest, influence, and potential impact to guide engagement strategy. Monitoring all stakeholders (A) comes later. Keeping all informed (C) is ongoing. Engaging stakeholders (D) follows analysis.

question_en: During a meeting with the customer, it was observed that the features delivered during the last few iterations were not meeting the planned expectations. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Review the requirements and instruct the team to develop the deliverables according to the documentation.
options_en.B: Mentor the team members and ensure they perform peer reviews of their work before implementation.
options_en.C: Utilize the retrospectives to identify issues in the development phase that may cause deliverables to not be accepted.
options_en.D: Ensure a continuous feedback environment is leveraged to improve the quality and overall satisfaction.

explanation_en: When features delivered during iterations are not meeting customer expectations, the root cause is typically a breakdown in feedback loops. The project manager should ensure a continuous feedback environment is leveraged to improve quality and overall satisfaction. Continuous feedback allows stakeholder input to be captured early and often, enabling course corrections before features are finalized. Reviewing requirements and instructing the team (A) is a top-down approach that does not address the underlying communication gap. Mentoring and peer reviews (B) improve internal quality but do not directly address customer expectation alignment. Retrospectives (C) are valuable but occur after the sprint; continuous feedback is more proactive and prevents dissatisfaction before it grows.

question_en: A company wants to show the commercial advantages of a product in a competitive market. They commissioned a project team to create a prototype. The team is building the prototype incrementally. What should the project manager set as a priority?

options_en.A: Implement the plan-do-check-action (PDCA) cycle.
options_en.B: Deliver business value as soon as possible.
options_en.C: Emphasize the use of Kanban methods.
options_en.D: Ensure that the project sponsor knows the schedule.

explanation_en: When a team is building a prototype incrementally to show commercial advantages in a competitive market, the project manager should prioritize delivering business value as soon as possible. Early value delivery enables market feedback. Implementing PDCA (A) is for continuous improvement, not prioritization. Emphasizing Kanban (C) addresses workflow visualization. Ensuring the sponsor knows the schedule (D) is communication, not prioritization.

question_en: A new project manager has been hired at a company that has suffered many project failures. The project manager has been tasked with delivering a software product for the company's biggest customer. The customer has not been able to articulate how a major piece of functionality should work. The project manager wants to deliver value immediately. How should the project manager approach the software development life cycle with this customer?

options_en.A: Raise a risk that scoping and estimating will be delayed if the customer cannot approve requirements
options_en.B: Explain that the team will build a production prototype model to help the customer visualize how the features should work
options_en.C: Assign a business analyst to build detailed requirements so the project manager can estimate the project duration
options_en.D: Add extra time and resources to the estimating phase to accommodate the lack of requirements

explanation_en: When a customer cannot clearly articulate how a major piece of functionality should work, the best approach is to build a production prototype model to help the customer visualize how the features should work. Prototyping makes requirements tangible, accelerates learning through rapid feedback, and reduces ambiguity by showing working behavior rather than relying on written specifications. This aligns with iterative delivery and progressive elaboration. Raising a scoping risk (A) documents uncertainty but does not solve the problem or create momentum. Assigning a business analyst for detailed requirements (C) still depends on the customer's ability to articulate needs. Adding extra time and resources to the estimating phase (D) delays value delivery without addressing the root cause.

question_en: A consultancy firm is finally selected and contracted for a project following an extensive and competitive procurement process. A few months into project execution, the client asks the project manager why the consultant is contracted for only 18 months instead of the full 32-month-long project. The project manager will need to carry out an unplanned second bidding process to ensure services are in place until the end of the project. What should the project manager have done to prevent this?

options_en.A: Prepared and negotiated a second contract with the consultancy firm for the remaining 14 months after the first contract signature.
options_en.B: Included the client in all negotiation phases with the consultancy to obtain their advanced approval before signing the contract.
options_en.C: Developed a detailed, phased procurement management plan including all activities required and had the client approve it.
options_en.D: Agreed beforehand with the client on the frequency of reporting on the status of the procurement activities within the project.

explanation_en: When a consultant was contracted for only 18 months of a 32-month project, requiring an unplanned second bidding process, the project manager should have developed a detailed, phased procurement management plan including all required activities and had the client approve it. Comprehensive procurement planning prevents gaps. Preparing a second contract after the first (A) is reactive. Including the client in negotiations (B) adds oversight but does not prevent the gap. Agreeing on procurement reporting frequency (D) is monitoring, not planning.

question_en: A project team member is struggling to understand a specific requirement. How should a servant leader address this issue?

options_en.A: Assist by connecting the product owner with the team member to discuss what problem is to be solved
options_en.B: Reassign the requirement to another team member who may have ideas on how to meet the requirement
options_en.C: Deprioritize the requirement and assign a task for it to be restated to provide the necessary clarity
options_en.D: Assess and evaluate the team member's skills to ensure alignment to the particular requirement and solution

explanation_en: When a team member struggles to understand a specific requirement, a servant leader should assist by connecting the product owner with the team member to discuss the problem. Facilitating direct communication with the requirement source addresses the root cause. Reassigning the requirement (B) avoids the issue. Deprioritizing it (C) delays resolution. Assessing the team member's skills (D) questions competence rather than clarifying the requirement.

question_en: Two team members are arguing about which technology they should use when implementing iteration tasks. The predictive approach was broken into several iterations that need to be completed on time so as not to jeopardize the project's timely completion. What should the project manager do to resolve this issue and help the team move on to the next iteration?

options_en.A: Allow the team to decide since the teams should be autonomous
options_en.B: Suggest their own approach to solve the issue and ask the team to follow it
options_en.C: Postpone the selection of the technology used until more information is gathered
options_en.D: Call for an open dialogue which the team will arrive at through consensus

explanation_en: When team members disagree on technology choices in a predictive project, the PM should facilitate open dialogue where everyone voices their opinions and concerns. Through collaborative discussion, the team can reach consensus, ensuring alignment and commitment. This approach resolves the immediate disagreement while fostering an inclusive, collaborative team environment essential for project success.

question_en: The team's work assignments have been generically distributed. A new team member is performing slower than expected. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Have all of the other team members retrain the new team member to improve team performance.
options_en.B: Extend the project timeline to allow the new team member to work at their own pace.
options_en.C: Assess the new team member's skills in order to determine additional training needs.
options_en.D: Change the way the work assignments are distributed to facilitate new team member development.

explanation_en: When a new team member with generic work assignments performs slower than expected, the project manager should assess the new member's skills to determine additional training needs. Skills assessment identifies the gap. Retraining by all other members (A) is disruptive. Extending the timeline (B) accepts inefficiency. Changing work distribution (D) may help but should follow assessment.

question_en: A project team member is sick and will not be able to return to the project for a few weeks. During the daily meeting, the team shares their concerns as the sick team member was the only one skilled in the component they were developing. What should the project manager have done to prevent this?

options_en.A: Requested robust documentation for the component's build.
options_en.B: Outsourced development of the specific component to another team.
options_en.C: Acquired more than one resource skilled in each component.
options_en.D: Facilitated cross-functional knowledge transfer during the project.

explanation_en: When a sick team member was the only one skilled in their component, the project manager should have facilitated cross-functional knowledge transfer during the project. Knowledge sharing prevents single points of failure. Requesting robust documentation (A) is partial. Outsourcing the component (B) does not build internal capability. Acquiring multiple skilled resources (C) is helpful but knowledge transfer is the more sustainable prevention.

question_en: An increment was delivered to the customer at the end of a sprint. The customer complains that the product does not meet the expected quality and will require some rework. What should the project manager do next?

options_en.A: Review the evidence of the quality assurance (QA) activities performed.
options_en.B: Include time in the next increment for quality assurance (QA) inspections.
options_en.C: Perform an analysis of the impact caused by the required rework.
options_en.D: Confirm with the customer the expected quality in the next increment.

explanation_en: When a customer complains that a delivered increment does not meet expected quality, the project manager should first review the evidence of QA activities performed. This determines whether the team followed agreed quality practices, met the Definition of Done, and executed required tests—identifying the root cause of the quality failure. Including time for QA inspections next increment (B) assumes more inspection is the solution without understanding the cause. Performing impact analysis (C) is important but premature without understanding why quality failed. Confirming expected quality with the customer (D) may be needed later but the immediate action is internal QA review.

question_en: A project manager is leading a highly visible project initiative. A few weeks after kickoff, the project manager starts receiving requests for updates from various stakeholders. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Remove those stakeholders from the project since they may negatively affect project goals
options_en.B: Invite all project stakeholders to join the daily standup meeting to ensure they are informed
options_en.C: Explain to the stakeholders that they must request project updates from the project sponsor
options_en.D: Schedule a meeting with relevant stakeholders to review the project communications plan

explanation_en: When receiving ad-hoc update requests from various stakeholders shortly after kickoff on a highly visible project, the project manager should schedule a meeting with relevant stakeholders to review the project communications plan. Aligning expectations prevents recurring requests. Removing stakeholders (A) is inappropriate. Inviting all to daily standups (B) disrupts team meetings. Directing stakeholders to the sponsor (C) creates bottlenecks.

question_en: A project manager must manage a virtual application control software team that is culturally and geographically diverse. The project manager wants to promote open collaboration in a real-time manner. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Document all information on the team wiki.
options_en.B: Facilitate regular conference calls.
options_en.C: Promote the use of remote site syndication.
options_en.D: Provide a software for instant messaging.

explanation_en: When managing a culturally and geographically diverse virtual team and wanting to promote real-time open collaboration, the project manager should provide instant messaging software. IM enables real-time, informal communication across time zones. Documenting on a team wiki (A) is asynchronous. Regular conference calls (B) are scheduled, not always real-time. Remote site syndication (C) is a content distribution method, not collaboration.

question_en: During project execution, the project manager notices that the work performance reports have deteriorated drastically in less than two weeks. The project team in country A is complaining about delays resulting from holidays occurring in country B that have impacted their project team. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options_en.A: Implement crashing to compress the schedule and improve the schedule performance index (SPI).
options_en.B: Review the risk management plan to evaluate the probability and impact of these delays
options_en.C: Perform conflict management using the project's resource management plan.
options_en.D: Implement fast-tracking to compress the schedule and improve the SPI

explanation_en: The project manager should review the risk management plan to evaluate the probability and impact of delays caused by holidays in country B. The risk management plan provides the framework for identifying, analyzing, and responding to project risks—including cross-cultural and scheduling factors inherent in multinational projects. By reviewing it, the PM can assess how these delays affect project objectives and select appropriate response strategies such as avoidance, mitigation, or acceptance. Implementing crashing (A) or fast-tracking (D) are schedule compression techniques that may increase costs, risks, or rework and do not address the root cause of the delays. Conflict management (C) is relevant for interpersonal disagreements but is not effective when the delays are caused by external factors like national holidays beyond the team's control.

question_en: A project manager realizes that the team members are new to the hybrid approach and do not value standup meetings. Team members often arrive late, digress into solutioning, or skip the meetings altogether. How should the project manager improve this situation with the project team?

options_en.A: Engage the project team in implementing and improving key aspects of the standup meetings.
options_en.B: Ask the product owner to remove team members who do not comply with standup meeting rules.
options_en.C: Send a daily retrospective report to all team members instead of holding standup meetings.
options_en.D: Include a daily brainstorming session in the standup meetings to resolve pending issues.

explanation_en: When team members do not value standup meetings, arrive late, digress, or skip them, the project manager should engage the team in implementing and improving key aspects of standups. Participatory improvement builds buy-in. Removing non-compliant members (B) is extreme. Sending retrospective reports instead (C) eliminates the standup's purpose. Adding brainstorming sessions (D) increases meeting scope.

question_en: A construction services company has influence within the local community with the potential to derail a project site establishment. Their bid was unsuccessful but they continue to communicate with the hope that their influence will persuade the project manager to reconsider their offer. What is the appropriate course of action for the project manager to pursue?

options_en.A: Reassess the bid to establish areas for improvement with the intention to assign work to this contractor
options_en.B: Meet with the unsuccessful bidder to review their submission and the areas that led to the bid being unsuccessful
options_en.C: Report the unsuccessful bidder to the local community leadership who have been supportive of the project
options_en.D: Do not communicate with the unsuccessful bidder as they do not have any further influence on the project

explanation_en: When an unsuccessful bidder continues to communicate hoping to influence the project manager, the appropriate action is to meet with them to review their submission and areas that led to the bid being unsuccessful. Transparent feedback maintains professional relationships and may benefit future projects. Reassessing the bid to assign work (A) undermines the procurement process. Reporting them to community leadership (C) is adversarial. Refusing all communication (D) damages relationships unnecessarily.

question_en: During the last two iterations of a project, one of the team members had low performance. The project manager conducted two feedback sessions with the team member and escalated the issue to the resource manager and project sponsor, but there has been no improvement. What should the project manager do next?

options_en.A: Review this obstacle during the daily standup meeting.
options_en.B: Escalate the situation again to the project sponsor.
options_en.C: Request a new resource to execute the activities.
options_en.D: Provide feedback to the resource at the sprint review.

explanation_en: When a team member's low performance persists after two feedback sessions and escalation to both the resource manager and sponsor, the project manager should request a new resource to execute the activities. Continued poor performance despite all corrective measures necessitates resource change to protect project objectives. Reviewing the obstacle at daily standup (A) revisits an already-addressed issue. Escalating to the sponsor again (B) repeats a step with no improvement. Providing sprint review feedback (D) is too late and ineffective.

question_en: An organization has historically executed most projects using a predictive approach. The organization now wants to change over to an agile approach. Which strategy will be useful to effectively help prepare the organization for this change?

options_en.A: Take a big bang approach of moving the whole organization to agile at once
options_en.B: Add multiple layers of managers who will be accountable for the agile execution
options_en.C: Create a task force of executives who will monitor agile projects on a daily basis
options_en.D: Improve organizational readiness by addressing impediments to agile in the organization.

explanation_en: The most effective strategy for transitioning from predictive to agile is improving organizational readiness by addressing impediments to agile adoption. Impediments may include cultural, structural, procedural, or technical barriers. By identifying and removing these obstacles, the organization creates a supportive environment for change—through training, coaching, cross-functional teams, and streamlined processes. A big bang approach (A) overwhelms the organization with change and ignores varying levels of readiness across departments. Adding management layers (B) creates bureaucracy that contradicts agile values of trust and empowerment. Creating an executive task force for daily monitoring (C) implies top-down control that conflicts with agile principles of team autonomy and self-organization.

question_en: A sales director is upset that progress has been slow on the delivery of critical features to the customer. After consulting with the team, the project manager learns that a subject matter expert (SME) on the customer side is not cooperative in providing the input needed to complete the definition of ready (DoR). What should the project manager do to avoid the same problem in future projects?

options_en.A: Rely on internal SMEs for expert input on implementing the user stories.
options_en.B: Include a contractual penalty for delays created by the customer.
options_en.C: Require customer SMEs to attend at least half of the daily meetings.
options_en.D: Review the responsibility matrix at the customer kick-off meeting.

explanation_en: The correct answer is D. The question asks how to avoid the same problem on future projects. The root cause is that customer SMEs did not understand or accept their responsibility to provide the information needed to meet the definition of ready. Reviewing the responsibility matrix (RACI) with the customer at the kickoff makes those roles explicit from the start. Relying on internal SMEs (A) cannot replace customer knowledge, contractual penalties (B) damage the relationship, and forcing SMEs to attend half of all daily meetings (C) is excessive and does not address their responsibility for DoR inputs.

question_en: A subcontractor informs the project manager that they are unable to supply a key component to the project. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Discuss the issue with the project sponsor and request extra time and budget to obtain the component from a different supplier.
options_en.B: Raise a new risk in the risk register, perform a risk assessment, and convene SMEs and relevant stakeholders to plan a risk response
options_en.C: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB) for changes to the performance measurement baseline to obtain the component from a different supplier.
options_en.D: Raise a new issue in the issue log and convene subject matter experts (SMEs) and relevant stakeholders to identify alternatives to address the problem.

explanation_en: When a subcontractor cannot supply a key component, the project manager should raise a new issue in the issue log and convene SMEs and relevant stakeholders to identify alternatives. This is an actual problem that has occurred and requires immediate issue resolution, not risk planning. Discussing with the sponsor for extra time and budget (A) is premature without exploring alternatives. Raising a risk in the risk register (B) treats it as a potential problem rather than an actual issue. Submitting a change request to the CCB (C) is a formal process that may not be necessary if alternatives exist.

question_en: A self-organizing team was delivering as committed. The team accepted a development task with new technology and the iterations started to have reduced velocity. What management decision is suited for this situation?

options_en.A: Re-assign the project to a team that has worked with this technology
options_en.B: Add new members to the team and increase the velocity
options_en.C: Move team members who are not performing from the team.
options_en.D: Provide opportunity for team members to learn and adjust to the technology.

explanation_en: When a self-organizing team's velocity drops after accepting a task with new technology, the appropriate decision is to provide opportunity for team members to learn and adjust to the technology. Learning time restores capability. Reassigning the project to another team (A) loses institutional knowledge. Adding new members (B) may introduce coordination overhead. Removing underperformers (C) is punitive and premature.

question_en: A project manager is leading a project team that consists of five team members. One of the team members, a senior technical staff member, always criticizes the ideas of other members during team meetings. However, this senior technical member is not performing well on their own daily tasks. Other team members are frustrated and have become silent in meetings. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Encourage other team members to provide one another with their valuable ideas.
options_en.B: Provide feedback to bring the team members' focus back to the performance of their daily tasks.
options_en.C: Reduce the team meeting frequency and seek input separately from team members.
options_en.D: Ask human resources (HR) to reassign the senior technical staff member.

explanation_en: When a senior technical member criticizes others' ideas while underperforming on their own tasks, causing frustration and silence, the project manager should provide feedback to bring focus back to daily task performance. Addressing behavior directly resolves the root cause. Encouraging other members' ideas (A) ignores the disruptive behavior. Reducing meeting frequency (C) avoids the problem. Asking HR to reassign (D) is extreme.

question_en: During iteration planning, team A identifies that an important deliverable is dependent upon a deliverable from team B. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Request team B to immediately start this activity and deliver to team A.
options_en.B: Make team A a part of team B and ensure that the deliverable is ready.
options_en.C: Ask team B to focus on their backlog and deliver based on their priority.
options_en.D: Inform team B of the dependency and ensure that the deliverable is planned.

explanation_en: When team A identifies a dependency on a deliverable from team B during iteration planning, the project manager should inform team B of the dependency and ensure the deliverable is planned accordingly. Proactive communication aligns both teams' efforts and schedules, avoiding delays. Requesting team B to start immediately (A) ignores team B's existing priorities and planning. Merging team A into team B (B) is disruptive and unnecessary for managing a single dependency. Asking team B to simply follow their own backlog priority (C) ignores the inter-team dependency and risks delays for team A.

question_en: A project manager wants to assign a junior engineer to a new project. In past projects, the engineer showed initiative to take on complex tasks and solve problems in innovative ways without any need for encouragement. During the last project, the engineer regularly worked late into the night for several months and told colleagues they felt exhausted. However, the engineer declines the project manager's invitation to join the new project. What is the most likely reason for the engineer's refusal to work on the project?

options_en.A: The engineer did not feel welcome or enjoy working with the other project team members.
options_en.B: The project manager did not sufficiently support and recognize the engineer's professional growth.
options_en.C: The engineer has "project burnout " from working long hours and solving difficult problems.
options_en.D: The project manager did not follow the normal hiring process with the engineer's functional manager.

explanation_en: The correct answer is C. The engineer worked long hours for months on difficult problems and said they felt exhausted, which are signs of project burnout. Nothing in the scenario suggests problems with team relationships (A), a lack of recognition (B), or a hiring-process issue (D). The project manager should explore the engineer's situation and consider workload and recovery time.

question_en: A company made several changes recently, which resulted in a positive change in the company culture. A project manager was just assigned to report to a new project supervisor whose leadership style is about getting things done quickly regardless of employee and operational impacts. Some employees are raising concerns about this. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Revisit the company's organizational culture.
options_en.B: Clarify expectations by explaining the company culture with the supervisor.
options_en.C: Instruct the employees to listen to the supervisor.
options_en.D: Ask senior management to move the supervisor to a different project.

explanation_en: The PM should clarify expectations by explaining the company culture to the new supervisor. This means communicating the positive cultural changes, how they affect project objectives and stakeholder satisfaction, and seeking to understand the supervisor's leadership style. Finding common ground that respects both organizational culture and supervisory authority is more constructive than requesting supervisor transfer, revisiting culture, or simply directing employees to comply.

question_en: A team member misses a project meeting without it being approved and has been penalized as defined in the ground rules. This team member, as well as other team members, insist that it is the first time they have seen this rule regarding the project and they do not agree with the penalty. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options_en.A: Ensured the team members are fully supportive of all decisions.
options_en.B: Ensured the team charter was developed by the team members
options_en.C: Used a charismatic leadership style
options_en.D: Distributed the project charter to all team members.

explanation_en: When a team member is penalized for missing a meeting per ground rules they claim not to have seen, the project manager should have ensured the team charter was developed by the team members. Team-developed charters create shared ownership of ground rules. Ensuring full support of all decisions (A) is impractical. Using a charismatic leadership style (C) does not address rule awareness. Distributing the project charter (D) is a one-way communication that may not ensure understanding.

question_en: During the course of the project, several obstacles are identified that are preventing the project from moving forward. What should the project manager do to remove the obstacles?

options_en.A: Implement plans to remove the obstacles
options_en.B: Have the project team work on other activities
options_en.C: Prioritize the obstacles for resolution
options_en.D: Escalate to the project steering committee

explanation_en: When obstacles are preventing the project from moving forward, the project manager should implement plans to remove the obstacles. Direct action resolves blockers. Having the team work on other activities (B) avoids the problem. Prioritizing obstacles (C) is necessary but insufficient without action. Escalating to the steering committee (D) is premature before attempting resolution.

question_en: Due to unforeseen circumstances, a contractor was unable to mobilize the project team, which was necessary to conduct face-to-face meetings and discussions. Virtual meetings were subsequently put in place, but the local project team and end users now face a communication gap that is causing the team's low performance. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Ask the contractor to solve this problem because this is a contractual obligation.
options_en.B: Terminate the contract and initiate a new one with a local contractor.
options_en.C: Reassess continually to remove blockers for the team.
options_en.D: Implement key performance indicators (KPIs) and convince the contractor to engage the team.

explanation_en: Virtual teams require the PM to actively manage communication and coordination challenges. The PM should continuously reassess the situation to identify and remove blockers hindering effective collaboration. While implementing KPIs can support performance monitoring, KPIs alone cannot resolve underlying communication issues. Terminating contracts or expecting contractors to solve problems independently contradicts the proactive, engaged management approach essential for virtual team success.

question_en: A Scrum team has information radiators but must also keep stakeholders aware of their progress. In addition, the project management office (PMO) has specific templates for status reporting to management. The project lead realizes that a variety of reporting will be needed to satisfy enterprise and stakeholder needs. What should the project lead do?

options_en.A: Document only the plan for written communications, and send meeting invites for verbal communication sessions.
options_en.B: Create a communications management plan informing all project team members and stakeholders who will receive what type of communication.
options_en.C: Follow the project management office (PMO) guidelines for communications instead of generating a project communications management plan.
options_en.D: Determine the minimum communications needed for the project, and adapt the communication plans as needed.

explanation_en: When a Scrum team must satisfy both agile information radiators and PMO-specific reporting templates, the project lead should create a communications management plan informing all team members and stakeholders who will receive what type of communication. This plan integrates agile practices with organizational requirements, ensuring comprehensive coverage. Documenting only written communications (A) is incomplete. Following only PMO guidelines (C) ignores project-specific needs. Determining minimum communications and adapting (D) may underserve stakeholder requirements.

question_en: During project execution, a project manager is informed that most of the project team members have enrolled in the newly implemented work-from-home company policy. How should the project manager reflect this change in the project?

options_en.A: Update roles and responsibilities for enrolled team members in the responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)
options_en.B: Update the resource calendar for enrolled team members in the resource management plan
options_en.C: Update the stakeholder engagement plan to include the emergency contact information for enrolled team members.
options_en.D: Update the communication styles for enrolled team members in the communications management plan.

explanation_en: When team members enroll in a work-from-home policy, the PM should update the resource calendar to reflect their availability and working hours. The resource calendar captures human and physical resource availability and may affect the project schedule, budget, quality, and risk. Communication styles, roles and responsibilities, and the stakeholder engagement plan are not directly impacted by this change in resource availability.

question_en: A project manager is working as a servant leader for a pilot project to adopt agile practices. After three sprints, the team demos the product to the main stakeholders, but receives negative feedback about the product's features. The team feels that all the features met the acceptance criteria defined by the product owner and does not understand what went wrong. How should the project manager mitigate the product rejection?

options_en.A: Engage the main stakeholders in the upcoming sprint review sessions.
options_en.B: Share the product backlog for the main stakeholders to review in advance.
options_en.C: Create dedicated sprints to implement feature fixes for the rejected ones.
options_en.D: Ask the project sponsor to evaluate the assignment of a new product owner.

explanation_en: When stakeholders give negative feedback at a demo despite features meeting acceptance criteria, the project manager should engage main stakeholders in upcoming sprint review sessions. Continuous stakeholder participation ensures alignment. Sharing the backlog for advance review (B) informs but does not engage. Creating dedicated fix sprints (C) is reactive. Evaluating a new product owner (D) assigns blame without evidence.

question_en: A project manager is managing a project that will handle sensitive data for millions of users. The sponsor mentioned that, to their knowledge, the project does not seem to have any compliance requirements in their country. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options_en.A: Trust in the expertise of the sponsor and believe that there are no compliance requirements for this project.
options_en.B: Request expert advice from the compliance leader to confirm if there are any compliance requirements for the project.
options_en.C: Conduct independent research regarding the data protection policy of the country for legal and regulatory compliance.
options_en.D: Check with the national compliance agency to determine if the project has any compliance requirements in this country

explanation_en: When the sponsor believes there are no compliance requirements for a project handling sensitive data for millions of users, the project manager should request expert advice from the compliance leader. The compliance leader has specialized knowledge to confirm or identify requirements the sponsor may have overlooked. Trusting the sponsor without verification (A) is risky. Conducting independent research (C) may be incomplete. Checking with the national agency (D) may miss organizational or regional requirements.

question_en: An agile team member discovers an impediment that is preventing them from doing their work efficiently. At which of the meetings should they bring up this impediment for resolution?

options_en.A: Daily Scrum meeting
options_en.B: Retrospective meeting
options_en.C: Sprint review meeting
options_en.D: Sprint planning meeting

explanation_en: The correct answer is A. Impediments should be raised as soon as possible, and the Daily Scrum is the daily opportunity for team members to share what is blocking them so it can be addressed quickly. Waiting for the retrospective (B), sprint review (C), or sprint planning (D) would delay resolution and slow the team's work.

question_en: A project manager is building a team to work on a service integration project that will transition technology management services from company A to company B. The project team will consist of members from both companies. Prospective team members for the project are located all over the world, have different types of technology backgrounds, and use different approaches for work. How should the project manager build a cohesive, high-performing team?

options_en.A: Organize the team members into several kick-off sessions based on technology type.
options_en.B: Ask prospective team members to write a short biography explaining how they can contribute to the team's success.
options_en.C: Review the list of team members' skills and understand how they will work together to deliver the project outcomes.
options_en.D: Ask the human resources (HR) department to arrange interview meetings to select the team.

explanation_en: When building a team from members across both companies with diverse backgrounds and approaches, the project manager should review team members' skills and understand how they will work together to deliver outcomes. Skill assessment aligns competencies with project needs and identifies how the team can collaborate effectively. Organizing kick-off sessions by technology type (A) may create silos. Requesting biographies (B) is subjective and incomplete. Having HR arrange interviews (D) delegates the PM's responsibility.

question_en: An organization is implementing a solar power system at its production plant. During the execution phase, one of the key stakeholders noticed and communicated that authorities are developing solar power regulation, which might impact the overall feasibility of the project. What should the project manager do first?

options_en.A: Put the project on hold and wait for the regulation information to be confirmed.
options_en.B: Meet with the sponsor to discuss the regulation issue and determine the proper action.
options_en.C: Proceed with the project as long as the regulation is not yet finalized.
options_en.D: Collect and analyze information about the new regulation.

explanation_en: The correct answer is D. Collect and analyze information about the new regulation. Risk and compliance management require proactive identification and assessment. The PM should evaluate impacts, follow proper processes, and implement appropriate response strategies.

question_en: A project manager received the project charter for a new product. The project is expected to have two main deliveries: the hardware part that has detailed specifications already defined, including a sample machine, and the user interface software that has only a basic specification and a requirement for a user experience design approach. Which project management approach should the project manager use?

options_en.A: The deliverables are significantly different, so the project should be split into two projects that are driven by a program.
options_en.B: The scope is well defined; therefore, a predictive approach is straightforward and the hardware and software can be synchronized on the gates.
options_en.C: The software development has a high uncertainty level, so an agile approach is recommended for the project.
options_en.D: A hybrid approach will work, using agile for software development and a predictive approach for the hardware deliveries.

explanation_en: When a project has hardware with detailed specifications and software with only basic specifications requiring UX design, the project manager should use a hybrid approach — agile for software development and predictive for hardware deliveries. This tailors the methodology to each deliverable's nature. Splitting into two program-driven projects (A) adds overhead. Using purely predictive (B) ignores software uncertainty. Using purely agile (C) is unsuitable for well-defined hardware.

question_en: A project manager is managing two agile teams and reviewing their metrics to find out which team is performing better. Which approach should be taken?

options_en.A: The issue should be addressed as part of a retrospective in the next iteration.
options_en.B: The velocity of both teams should be compared at the end of every iteration.
options_en.C: The team with the higher velocity is performing better and should be rewarded.
options_en.D: The velocity should not be compared as teams can size items differently.

explanation_en: Velocity should not be compared between agile teams because teams size items differently. Velocity measures the amount of work a team completes in a given period—not the quality or value of that work. Cross-team velocity comparisons lead to inaccurate conclusions and unhealthy competition. Instead, the PM should use each team's velocity for their own planning and forecasting, and focus on outcome-based metrics that reflect project benefits and value delivery.

question_en: After difficult negotiations, a customer committed to pay the cost for changes to the project scope. The team seems unhappy as the project completion time will take longer than previously scheduled. How should the project manager support the outcome of the new agreement?

options_en.A: Find a way to maintain the project schedule.
options_en.B: Impose authority on the project.
options_en.C: Request additional resources from the sponsor and motivate the team.
options_en.D: Motivate the team and deploy the necessary resources.

explanation_en: When the customer agrees to pay for scope changes but the team is unhappy about the extended timeline, the project manager should motivate the team and deploy the necessary resources. Acknowledgment, communication, and adequate resourcing support morale and execution. Finding a way to maintain the original schedule (A) may compromise quality. Imposing authority (B) creates resentment. Requesting additional resources from the sponsor (C) duplicates the resource deployment and adds unnecessary motivation as a separate action.

question_en: During the executing phase, a project manager is reviewing the issue log and finds there are outstanding high-priority issues that are still open. Most of the open issues require effort from external domain experts who are not on the project team. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Request that the project team members learn the required domain knowledge and resolve the open issues in a short time.
options_en.B: Ask the issue reporter to close the issues, because there are no project team members who have the required domain knowledge.
options_en.C: Reduce the project scope to ensure that the project team has the knowledge to deliver the system on schedule.
options_en.D: Review the open issues with the issue reporter and issue a change request to hire an external domain expert.

explanation_en: When outstanding high-priority issues require external domain experts not on the project team, the project manager should review the open issues with the reporter and issue a change request to hire an external domain expert. This addresses the knowledge gap through formal change control. Requesting the team learn domain knowledge quickly (A) is unrealistic. Asking the reporter to close issues (B) ignores them. Reducing project scope (C) compromises deliverables.

question_en: A company is transitioning their projects to utilize hybrid project management approaches. While putting together their project team, the project manager discovers the requirements from the customer are unclear and also realizes that the team members are lacking critical technical skills needed for project success. However, the customer will not accept any changes to the requirements. What should the project manager do to resolve this issue?

options_en.A: Find and provide training to the project team members who do not have the required skills
options_en.B: Ask the scrum master to refine the user stories to improve the team members' understanding
options_en.C: Submit a change request to adapt the objectives of the project to the current situation
options_en.D: Extend the duration of standup meetings to include skill transference from trained to untrained members

explanation_en: When team members lack critical technical skills needed for project success, the project manager should find and provide relevant training to bridge the skill gap. This ensures the team has the necessary competencies to deliver on project objectives, even when requirements are unclear. Training aligns with hybrid project management principles of continuous learning and adaptability. Asking the scrum master to refine user stories (B) may clarify requirements but does not address the technical skills gap. Submitting a change request to adapt project objectives (C) assumes the situation is unresolvable through capability building. Extending standup meetings for skill transfer (D) is not an effective training mechanism and disrupts the purpose of daily standups.

question_en: A project manager is working on an enterprise resource planning (ERP) initiative that contains stakeholders spanning numerous business lines. The project manager begins to identify, evaluate, and categorize the stakeholder relationships to the program. What is the purpose of this process?

options_en.A: Incorporate only primary stakeholders into the communications management plan.
options_en.B: Identify all stakeholders who can positively affect the project.
options_en.C: Incorporate the needs of all stakeholders into the communications management plan.
options_en.D: Identify all stakeholders who can negatively affect the project.

explanation_en: When identifying, evaluating, and categorizing stakeholder relationships in an ERP initiative spanning numerous business lines, the purpose is to incorporate the needs of all stakeholders into the communications management plan. Comprehensive understanding enables tailored engagement. Incorporating only primary stakeholders (A) excludes important groups. Identifying only positive stakeholders (B) or only negative stakeholders (D) provides incomplete analysis.

question_en: In a global project, the main definitions were developed in country A, and the delivery of the project will be completed in phases in countries B, C, and D. Country B discovers that one of the legal requirements was not addressed. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options_en.A: Identified the regulatory differences among the countries.
options_en.B: Managed risk mitigation strategies specific to each country.
options_en.C: Selected countries that had similar regulatory requirements.
options_en.D: Asked procurement to assign resources located in each country.

explanation_en: When country B discovers a missed legal requirement in a global project planned in country A, the project manager should have identified the regulatory differences among the countries. Comprehensive regulatory analysis prevents compliance gaps. Managing country-specific risk mitigation (B) is reactive. Selecting countries with similar regulations (C) is impractical. Assigning local resources via procurement (D) does not ensure regulatory compliance.

question_en: A new employee has joined the management team and wants to get a quick overview of all the agile team's projects. What should the agile team lead recommend to the employee as a first step to gain this understanding?

options_en.A: Connect with each project's scrum master to assess progress.
options_en.B: Meet with each project's development team separately.
options_en.C: Review the information radiators for each project.
options_en.D: Attend the daily standup meetings for each project.

explanation_en: When a new management team employee wants a quick overview of all agile projects, the agile team lead should recommend reviewing information radiators for each project. Information radiators—such as burndown charts, kanban boards, and sprint boards—are visual tools designed for quick, transparent status communication accessible to all stakeholders. Connecting with each scrum master (A) is less efficient for a first overview. Meeting each development team separately (B) is time-consuming. Attending daily standups (D) provides insight but requires daily commitment and is less efficient initially.

question_en: A project manager has been assigned with initiating a large project to deliver complex equipment. Part of the project will be the result of a long research process, but once this is completed, the other part of the project must be incrementally delivered to the customer. Which approach should the project manager choose for this project?

options_en.A: Hybrid
options_en.B: Predictive
options_en.C: Waterfall
options_en.D: Agile

explanation_en: For a project that begins with a long research process followed by incremental delivery to the customer, the project manager should choose a hybrid approach. A hybrid approach combines predictive and adaptive methodologies, allowing the PM to apply a predictive method for the research phase—where scope, schedule, and cost are well-defined—and an agile approach for the delivery phase, where iterative releases and frequent customer feedback are essential. A purely predictive (B), waterfall (C), or agile (D) approach would not adequately address the project's dual nature of structured research followed by flexible, incremental delivery.

question_en: A project team is working remotely on a solution. The client wants the solution as soon as possible and is uncomfortable because the team members are not colocated. In addition, the client expressed concerns about the understanding of the project context and the team's decision-making process. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Encourage the client to interact with the project collaboration platform
options_en.B: Update the communications management plan to satisfy the client's request
options_en.C: Ask the product owner to frequently communicate with the stakeholders
options_en.D: Request the client to attend the daily meetings with the project team

explanation_en: When a remote team's client is uncomfortable with the lack of colocation and concerned about context understanding and decision-making, the project manager should update the communications management plan to satisfy the client's request. Enhanced communication planning addresses transparency and trust. Encouraging platform interaction (A) is vague. Asking the product owner to communicate more (C) delegates PM responsibility. Requesting client attendance at daily meetings (D) may be excessive.

question_en: A project manager is closing a project and preparing to hand it over to the operations team. During handover, a delayed invoice was submitted with a higher-than-planned cost against the project work. Consequently, project handover was delayed and the project's reported completion costs were increased. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options_en.A: Involved the finance team and discussed the issue with the vendor
options_en.B: Reviewed the total committed cost against the cost invoiced at project closing
options_en.C: Notified all vendors about the invoicing and nonpayment deadlines
options_en.D: Captured and reviewed all of the project work and related costs regularly

explanation_en: To avoid delayed invoices with unexpected costs at project closing, the project manager should have captured and reviewed all project work and related costs regularly throughout the project lifecycle. Regular monitoring enables early detection of discrepancies and timely corrective actions, preventing surprises during handover. Involving the finance team and discussing with the vendor (A) is reactive rather than preventive. Reviewing total committed cost against invoiced cost at closing (B) is a closing activity that comes too late to prevent the issue. Notifying vendors about invoicing deadlines (C) is helpful but insufficient without the internal discipline of regular cost monitoring.

question_en: A project manager is working on a highly complex project. During the execution of the project, the local government changed certain environmental regulations, which could potentially delay the project. What immediate action should the project manager take?

options_en.A: Update the change request log.
options_en.B: Update the risk management plan.
options_en.C: Update the project baseline.
options_en.D: Update the issue log.

explanation_en: When the local government changes environmental regulations during project execution, this is an issue that has already occurred—not a future risk. The project manager's immediate action should be to update the issue log to document and track this external factor, its potential impact on the project, and the planned resolution. Updating the change request log (A) is premature—the issue needs to be documented first before determining if a change request is required. Updating the risk management plan (B) addresses processes, not the specific current event. Updating the project baseline (C) can only be done through formal change control and is not an immediate first step.

question_en: During an iteration demo, a customer noticed an enhancement they would like to make to the product. What should the team do next?

options_en.A: Refine and estimate the enhancement so the size is known.
options_en.B: Add it to the product backlog to be completed in the future.
options_en.C: Ask the product owner to prioritize the item with the customer.
options_en.D: Start working on the enhancement for the customer immediately.

explanation_en: When a customer notices a desired enhancement during an iteration demo, the team should ask the product owner to prioritize the item with the customer. The product owner manages backlog priority and customer needs. Refining and estimating the enhancement (A) is premature without prioritization. Adding to the backlog without prioritization (B) skips value assessment. Starting work immediately (D) bypasses the product owner's authority.

question_en: The project manager just started leading a project team from which the previous project manager resigned. After a quick evaluation of the project, it is apparent that team morale is low due to continuous disagreement about how to complete tasks. Tasks are taking longer than forecasted and the project is off schedule. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Crash the project timeline to ensure the project is back on schedule
options_en.B: Issue a change request to extend the project schedule based on identified delays
options_en.C: Conduct a meeting with the project team to discuss and address the sources of disagreement
options_en.D: Inform the stakeholders that the project will be delayed due to previous team management

explanation_en: When team morale is low due to continuous disagreement about task completion methods and the project is off schedule, the project manager should conduct a meeting with the team to discuss and address the sources of disagreement. Direct conflict resolution identifies root causes and fosters collaborative solutions. Crashing the timeline (A) adds pressure without addressing morale. Issuing a change request to extend the schedule (B) accepts the situation. Informing stakeholders of delay (D) communicates without resolving.

question_en: Two team members are consistently having misunderstandings and find it difficult to work together. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options_en.A: Warn the team members about their behavior
options_en.B: Train the team members on communication techniques and interpersonal behavior
options_en.C: Remove one of the team members
options_en.D: Identify the issues between the team members and guide them toward a resolution

explanation_en: When two team members consistently have misunderstandings and find it difficult to work together, the project manager should identify the issues between them and guide them toward a resolution. Using collaborative conflict resolution techniques addresses root causes and fosters a positive team environment. Warning about behavior (A) does not address underlying issues. Training on communication techniques (B) is general and may not resolve specific interpersonal conflict. Removing a team member (C) is an extreme measure that avoids resolution.

question_en: An agile senior project team member suddenly resigns from the organization. Following this departure, the remaining team members are having difficulty accessing information and are unable to complete a deliverable. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options_en.A: Provided specialist training for all team members.
options_en.B: Updated the job descriptions for all team roles.
options_en.C: Ensured the project repository is up to date.
options_en.D: Made an effort to reemploy the senior project team member.

explanation_en: When a senior agile team member's sudden resignation causes the remaining team to lose access to information, the project manager should have ensured the project repository was up to date. Centralized documentation prevents knowledge silos. Specialist training (A) builds skills but does not capture knowledge. Updating job descriptions (B) is administrative. Trying to rehire the member (D) is reactive.

question_en: A project manager is transferred to another country to perform a project within their organization. What should the project manager do first to ensure collaboration within the team for a successful delivery?

options_en.A: Mentor the team members to perform project management.
options_en.B: Assign a local resource to manage communication with the team.
options_en.C: Determine a leadership style that is suitable for that location.
options_en.D: Check if resources from headquarters can also be assigned to the project.

explanation_en: When transferred to another country for a project, the project manager should first determine a leadership style suitable for that location. Different cultures have varying preferences for communication, decision-making, power distance, and teamwork. Adapting leadership style ensures effective collaboration with the local team. Mentoring team members in project management (A) develops skills but does not address cultural adaptation. Assigning a local resource for communication (B) delegates rather than adapts. Checking if headquarters resources can be assigned (D) does not address the cultural adaptation need.

question_en: A project manager has been managing a highly complex project. The project manager has ensured that all of the required tasks have been completed. During a recent external audit, the project manager was informed of a heavy penalty being levied on the project for the latest module that was implemented. What should the project manager have done to ensure that there were no liabilities arising from the recent implementation?

options_en.A: Ensured that all the required approvals were received per the organizational procedures
options_en.B: Ensured that all documentation was completed post implementation before closing the project
options_en.C: Ensured that all of the required tasks identified in the scope were completed successfully
options_en.D: Ensured that all defects identified during testing were resolved before implementation

explanation_en: When an external audit levied a heavy penalty for a recently implemented module, the project manager should have ensured all required approvals were received per organizational procedures. Proper approvals prevent compliance liabilities. Completing documentation post-implementation (B) is too late. Completing tasks identified in scope (C) does not ensure compliance. Resolving defects before implementation (D) addresses quality, not procedural compliance.

question_en: The project team is conducting iteration planning and having difficulty evaluating a new technology that will be used in this iteration. What should the project lead do?

options_en.A: Hire an external subject matter expert (SME) to help with design and implementation.
options_en.B: Coach the team to determine a path forward to achieve an efficient solution.
options_en.C: Provide technical guidance on complexity assessment.
options_en.D: Guide the team with estimating the time required.

explanation_en: The correct answer is B. The team is struggling to evaluate a new technology during planning. A servant-leader project lead should coach the team to find its own path forward, such as running a spike or researching options, which builds capability and ownership. Hiring an external SME (A) may be unnecessary, and giving technical guidance (C) or estimates (D) takes over decisions the team should make.

question_en: A new agile project manager is trying to determine how the team is performing against the schedule for a release. Which tool will provide a deeper look into the team's progress?

options_en.A: Kanban board
options_en.B: Product roadmap
options_en.C: Release plan
options_en.D: Burndown chart

explanation_en: When an agile project manager needs a deeper look into team progress against the release schedule, a burndown chart provides the most detailed view. It shows remaining work versus time, revealing trends and pace. A Kanban board (A) shows workflow status, not schedule progress. A product roadmap (B) shows high-level milestones. A release plan (C) outlines planned iterations but lacks real-time progress tracking.

question_en: A project team has been working together for about 2 years. One of the team members has consistently shown high performance and stood out among their peers during the execution of the project. How should the project manager recognize high performance?

options_en.A: Ask the sponsor to approve a bonus for the high-performing team member.
options_en.B: Thank the team member privately to avoid conflict among the team members.
options_en.C: Choose a reward for the team member that aligns with their personal goals.
options_en.D: Acknowledge the high-performing team member in the next team meeting.

explanation_en: When a team member has consistently shown high performance over 2 years, the project manager should choose a reward that aligns with the team member's personal goals. Personalized recognition is the most effective motivator. Asking the sponsor for a bonus (A) is one approach but may not be available. Thanking privately (B) avoids team acknowledgment. Acknowledging in a team meeting (D) is good but may not align with individual preferences.

question_en: A project team has difficulty understanding the relationship between functional requirements and their associated benefit to the business stakeholders. How should the project manager improve the team's understanding?

options_en.A: Involve team members in stakeholder analysis and engagement.
options_en.B: Engage with the project sponsor and ensure the product backlog is correct and up to date.
options_en.C: Ensure team members have access to a well-written requirements traceability matrix.
options_en.D: Invite all stakeholders to progress meetings to avoid ambiguity.

explanation_en: When the team has difficulty understanding the relationship between functional requirements and their business benefits, the project manager should ensure team members have access to a well-written requirements traceability matrix. The RTM explicitly connects requirements to business needs, stakeholder goals, and objectives. Involving team members in stakeholder analysis (A) is helpful but indirect. Engaging the sponsor for backlog updates (B) addresses content but not traceability. Inviting stakeholders to progress meetings (D) provides exposure but not structured understanding.

question_en: A project has a very demanding and sensitive business stakeholder who functions as a subject matter expert (SME). The project manager has assigned two different team members to work with the stakeholder. However, both team members have complained that the stakeholder is difficult to work with. What should the project manager do first?

options_en.A: Escalate the issue to the sponsor and request that they speak with the stakeholder.
options_en.B: Speak with the team members to collect details and write an email to the stakeholder requesting that they collaborate with the team.
options_en.C: Raise the issue during a steering committee meeting and ask that the stakeholder change their attitude.
options_en.D: Evaluate the situation and look for alternatives to improve communication with the stakeholder.

explanation_en: When two team members report that a demanding SME stakeholder is difficult to work with, the project manager should first evaluate the situation and look for alternatives to improve communication with the stakeholder. Understanding before acting enables constructive resolution. Escalating to the sponsor (A) bypasses direct resolution. Writing an email requesting collaboration (B) is impersonal. Raising it in a steering committee (C) is confrontational and premature.

question_en: A project manager has been assigned to a project. The project deadline has been established but, based on the number of stakeholders to engage and interview, it will be difficult to complete the project within the timeline. How should the project manager address this challenge?

options_en.A: Request that the product owner define which parties should be engaged first.
options_en.B: Prioritize the engagement of parties who are most impacted to minimize project risk.
options_en.C: Submit a change request to extend the time needed to engage all of the parties.
options_en.D: Commit to completing the deliverables associated with only the engaged parties.

explanation_en: When the project timeline is tight relative to the number of stakeholders requiring engagement, the project manager should prioritize engagement based on impact and risk. Engaging the most impacted parties first ensures the project captures critical requirements, constraints, and acceptance conditions from those who most influence success or failure. Requesting the product owner to define engagement priorities (A) does not replace the PM's responsibility to analyze and plan stakeholder engagement. Submitting a change request to extend time (C) may eventually be needed but should not be the first action—optimizing engagement within existing constraints comes first. Committing to deliverables only for engaged parties (D) risks missing requirements and leads to poor adoption and stakeholder dissatisfaction.

question_en: A project manager has recently been assigned to an agile project and discovers that a contractor for the project does not have any experience with agile. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Ask the project sponsor to replace the contractor since they do not have agile experience
options_en.B: Issue a formal notice to the contractor to obtain an agile certification
options_en.C: Consult the project team to understand the extent of the training needs for the contractor
options_en.D: Instruct the contractor to receive agile training since the project has already started

explanation_en: When a contractor on an agile project lacks agile experience, the project manager should consult the project team to understand the extent of training needs for the contractor. Collaborative assessment ensures targeted support. Asking the sponsor to replace the contractor (A) causes unnecessary delays. Issuing a formal notice for certification (B) creates distrust. Instructing training without team input (D) may not address specific project needs.

question_en: There is a problem with a project because some features are not in compliance with regulations. Some stakeholders do not believe compliance is a priority, while others disagree. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Set up some time with the stakeholders to explain the importance of compliance.
options_en.B: Send out documentation to align stakeholder expectations and project objectives.
options_en.C: Review the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix to determine next steps.
options_en.D: Meet with the sponsor to discuss how to handle the stakeholders' differing opinions.

explanation_en: The correct answer is A. Some stakeholders do not see compliance as a priority. Meeting them to explain the importance of compliance, including legal and business consequences, is the most effective way to align them. Sending documentation (B) is one-way, reviewing the assessment matrix (C) does not change their view, and meeting the sponsor (D) bypasses the stakeholders.

question_en: A project manager has noticed that the performance of a new team member has increased dramatically over the past few months. The project manager has been measuring this team member's performance through the cost performance index (CPI) and schedule performance index (SPI) of work packages. The project manager has also assigned new, unrelated work packages to this team member. The project manager wants to formally record the team member's success in the project documentation. What should the project manager do?

options_en.A: Attach a note to the project management plan about the team member
options_en.B: Hold a project team meeting about the team member's contribution and take minutes
options_en.C: Record the team member's contribution in the responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)
options_en.D: Send a communication to management recognizing the team member's contributions

explanation_en: When the project manager wants to formally record a new team member's dramatically improved performance, they should send a communication to management recognizing the team member's contributions. Formal communication ensures recognition reaches leadership. Attaching a note to the project management plan (A) is informal. Holding a team meeting (B) celebrates but does not document formally. Recording in the RAM (C) assigns responsibilities, not performance recognition.

question_en: A team member is openly criticized by others during a standup meeting for failing to complete yesterday's tasks. What should the agile coach do first to address the situation?

options_en.A: Address the team members involved during the next sprint retrospective.
options_en.B: Avoid the discussion by referring to the team charter.
options_en.C: Emphasize the ground rules and then focus on today's activities and impediments.
options_en.D: Let the discussion go on as it is important that the team is clear on priorities for the day.

explanation_en: When a team member is publicly criticized during a standup, the agile coach should intervene immediately. The coach should reinforce meeting ground rules—mutual respect, supportive behavior, and focus on the work—then redirect the team's attention to current activities and impediments. This prevents conflict escalation, maintains a positive team atmosphere, and keeps the team progressing. Letting the discussion continue, deferring to the retrospective, or avoiding the issue by referencing the team charter are all ineffective responses that may ignore, postpone, or evade the problem.

question_en: A project to develop an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system for a university is ongoing. The system should improve business processes through digitalization and elimination of human errors, and also provide end users with simplified and easily accessible services. What should the project manager do to ensure achievement of the intended business value?

options_en.A: Evaluate deliverables against the business case at the end of the life cycle
options_en.B: Evaluate customer feedback and review the business case each time
options_en.C: Evaluate deliverables against the business case continuously
options_en.D: Evaluate each change request and review the business case each time

explanation_en: When an ERP project aims to improve processes and reduce errors, the project manager should evaluate deliverables against the business case continuously to ensure intended business value. Continuous validation enables early detection of misalignment. Evaluating only at the end (A) is too late. Evaluating with each change request (D) is reactive. Combining customer feedback with reviews (B) is useful but continuous evaluation is the primary approach.

question_en: A project has issues arising where the data integration team and the data migration team have areas that overlap. It is not clear who would be responsible for delivery on these areas. What should the project manager do next?

options_en.A: Review the work breakdown structure (WBS) to align the project teams
options_en.B: Review the resource management plan to align the project teams
options_en.C: Review the project scope to align the project teams
options_en.D: Review the project integration plan to align the project teams

explanation_en: When data integration and data migration teams have overlapping areas with unclear delivery responsibility, the project manager should review the WBS to align the project teams. The WBS clarifies work decomposition and responsibility boundaries. Reviewing the resource management plan (B) addresses people, not work scope. Reviewing the project scope (C) is broader than needed. Reviewing the integration plan (D) addresses dependencies, not task ownership.

question_en: After 1 year into the life cycle of an ongoing residential project, an announcement was received from the municipality regarding a new regulation that will greatly impact the project's schedule and budget. What should the project manager do next?
